summary:
Recap of an Allwork.Space Future of Work podcast episode with Darren Murph, distributed work expert, founder of Page 52 Consulting and former workplace strategy leader at GitLab, where he helped build the operating model for a fully distributed workforce.

Core argument: remote work is no longer about where people sit but whether companies have the systems, processes and operational discipline to support teams that never share an office. Murph likens a remote organization to an "invisible skyscraper": even without a building, the company still needs the equivalent of workplace infrastructure, including clear processes, communication systems, documentation and shared expectations. Sending people home with laptops was never sufficient.

Knowledge management is framed as newly critical in the AI era. Distributed companies were forced to document because informal office conversation was unavailable, and that habit now pays off: without centralized knowledge, AI tools give unreliable answers because information sits on individual devices, in conversations, or on disconnected platforms. Organized information becomes the foundation for AI adoption.

Hiring is shifting from cultural fit toward operational fit, meaning whether someone can work within systems based on documentation, asynchronous communication and defined processes. Supporting practices include meeting guidelines, team agreements, written goals and communication expectations. Managers do not need company-wide change; individual teams can set their own agreements on tools, response times and workflows.

On workspace, Murph notes not everyone wants to work from home; some want separation of living and working space, creating an opening for coworking. Coworking stipends are offered as a way to give employees choice while staying remote-first.

Finally, AI plus remote work is lowering barriers for solo entrepreneurs and small teams to do work that once needed larger headcount, suggesting more businesses may stay small, built on specialized expertise, technology and strong operational systems. Flexibility alone is not enough without infrastructure behind it.

claims.claim: Effective distributed work requires an "invisible skyscraper" of processes, communication systems, documentation and shared expectations rather than just sending employees home with laptops.
claims.attribution: Darren Murph, founder of Page 52 Consulting and former GitLab workplace strategy leader

Without centralized knowledge, AI systems may give inaccurate answers because information is scattered across individual devices, conversations and disconnected platforms.
Companies are increasingly hiring for operational fit rather than only cultural alignment.
Coworking stipends let companies give employees workspace choice while remaining remote-first.
The combination of remote work and AI is lowering barriers for solo entrepreneurs and small teams to do work that previously required larger teams.
Murph helped build the operating model behind GitLab's fully distributed workforce.
